newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus hails landmark Eurocourt ruling on Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus hails landmark Eurocourt ruling on Turkey.

text.p: Cyprus greeted a ruling by the European Court of Human Rights against Turkey for violating the property rights of a Greek Cypriot as a landmark judgment that could open the floodgates to demands for compensation arising from the 1974 invasion.
"It is a great success," Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides said of Wednesday's ruling.

In a case watched closely by Cyprus, the Strasbourg Court ruled by 11 votes to six that Turkey had violated Titina Loizidou's property rights by denying her access to her plots of land in Turkish-occupied Kyrenia in northern Cyprus.

Cypriot lawyers said the ruling had important political implications by making Turkey responsible for the situation on the island, not the breakaway Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus declared in 1983 and recognised only by Ankara.
"I believe its effects can be enormous," said Clerides. "If we take into account those who were forced to leave their homes then the effects can be greater."
Some 200,000 Greek Cypriots were displaced in the Turkish invasion of the northern third of the island which was sparked by a brief coup engineered by the military regime then in power in Greece.
The ruling gave Turkey six months to submit observations on Loizidou's claim for compensation. Her lawyers are seeking up to half a million Cyprus pounds ($1.07 million) in damages.
Acceptance of compensation does not affect Loizidou's ownership rights, said her lawyer Achilleas Demetriades.

When she tried to return to Kyrenia in March 1989 with a Greek Cypriot group called "Women Walk Home", she was arrested by Turkish Cypriot police in Nicosia and returned via United Nations officials to the Greek Cypriot sector.
"It is a landmark case in human rights and in the history of international law," said Cypriot Attorney-General Alecos Markides.
"The importance of this decision is that it is acknowledged Turkey is responsible for the violation of human rights in the occupied areas because it controls the situation there."
Other Greek Cypriot applications against Turkey were pending in Strasbourg, Markides said. "This was a test case and they were awaiting the result," he said.
